question: What is the main focus of critical care in the community setting?

options.A: Conducting clinical drug trials in large urban tertiary hospitals
options.B: Performing complex elective surgeries in rural primary health centers
options.C: Delivering life-saving interventions outside traditional hospital intensive care units
options.D: Managing chronic stable illnesses during routine home visits

explanation: You don't always need a big hospital ICU to save a life! Community critical care is all about bringing quick emergency help right to primary clinics and homes. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h1)

question: Why is the community nurse so vital in settings with limited resources?

options.A: They replace the need for any secondary or tertiary healthcare facilities
options.B: They have unlimited access to advanced mechanical ventilators and dialysis machines
options.C: They serve as the first line of defense to stabilize rapidly deteriorating patients before hospital transfer
options.D: They are the only healthcare workers legally permitted to perform major surgeries

explanation: Spotting danger signs early and starting care right away makes all the difference when a patient arrives at a local clinic first. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h1)

question: On the AVPU neurological scale, what does the letter 'V' stand for?
explanation: Remember AVPU: Alert, Voice-responsive, Pain-responsive, and Unresponsive. It's a quick and handy way to check mental status! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h2)

question: A patient is breathing rapidly at 34 breaths per minute and straining their neck muscles to breathe. What should you do right away?

options.A: Document the findings as normal vital signs for an adult and schedule a routine follow-up
options.B: Recognize this as severe respiratory distress and prepare immediate oxygen and triage support
options.C: Advise the patient to lie flat on their back and sleep off the exhaustion
options.D: Administer an oral antipyretic medication for presumed fever

explanation: Using accessory neck muscles and breathing super fast are clear SOS signs of severe breathing trouble. Time to act fast with oxygen! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h2)

question: What is the first step when a patient's airway is blocked by secretions in a community clinic?

options.B: Starting an immediate intravenous infusion of normal saline
options.C: Clearing the airway using proper positioning and suctioning

explanation: Airway comes first in every emergency! Positioning the patient and clearing out any blockage gets them breathing easier. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h3)

question: When would a nurse use the intraosseous (IO) route for giving fluids?

options.A: As the routine first choice for every patient needing oral medication
options.B: When the patient refuses to take medications by mouth
options.C: When peripheral veins cannot be accessed quickly in a severe shock emergency
options.D: Only after the patient has fully recovered and is ready for discharge

explanation: When shock hits and veins collapse, going straight into the bone marrow (IO) is a lifesaver for getting fluids in fast. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h3)

question: Which drug is given immediately for a patient experiencing severe anaphylactic shock?
explanation: Epinephrine given in the muscle acts fast to open up airways and reverse dangerous swelling and drops in blood pressure. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h4)

question: A new mother at a health post starts bleeding heavily and looks dizzy and pale. What are your first nursing steps?

options.A: Encourage the patient to stand up and walk around to stimulate circulation
options.B: Apply a warm compress to the patient's forehead and offer oral fluids
options.C: Wait quietly for two hours to see if the bleeding stops on its own
options.D: Perform uterine massage, give oxytocin, and prepare for emergency referral

explanation: Postpartum hemorrhage is an emergency. Massaging the uterus and giving oxytocin helps it contract while you arrange urgent transfer. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h4)

question: How can nurses safely manage IV fluids when electronic infusion pumps aren't available?

options.A: By using gravity drip sets paired with frequent manual monitoring of flow rates
options.B: By clamping the intravenous line completely shut for hours at a time
options.C: By squeezing the intravenous fluid bag continuously by hand until empty
options.D: By substituting all intravenous therapy with oral water ingestion

explanation: Gravity infusion sets plus regular, careful checks help nurses control flow safely even without fancy hospital equipment. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a safe clinical improvisation in a rural clinic?

options.A: Reusing disposable single-use syringes across multiple patients to save costs
options.B: Using clean wooden boards and cloth wraps as temporary limb splints
options.C: Relying on solar-powered generators to run oxygen concentrators
options.D: Using gravity infusion sets with frequent manual checks for fluid delivery

explanation: Never reuse single-use needles or syringes! That's a major infection risk that puts patients in grave danger. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h5)

question: What vital paper must always travel with a critically ill patient during a transfer?

options.A: A blank sheet of paper for the driver to take notes on
options.B: A detailed referral note outlining history, vital signs, and treatments given
options.C: The personal identity card of the attending nurse
options.D: A receipt for the purchase of hospital drugs

explanation: The receiving team needs to know what happened so far, what vital signs look like, and what drugs were given. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h6)

question: Why should you always call the receiving hospital before transferring a patient?

options.A: To ask the receiving hospital for permission to discharge the patient home
options.B: To ensure the receiving team is prepared and has the necessary bed and staff ready
options.C: To negotiate the cost of fuel for the transport vehicle
options.D: To verify if the patient has paid their hospital registration fees

explanation: A quick call ahead ensures the team is waiting with a bed and ready to take over critical care without wasting a second. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h6)

question: What is the main goal of nursing care for a patient with an irreversible, end-stage illness at home?

options.B: Transferring the patient to a busy surgical intensive care unit
options.D: Providing comfort, pain relief, and emotional support

explanation: When cure isn't possible, palliative care focuses on keeping the patient comfortable, managing pain, and preserving dignity. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h7)

question: How does your nursing focus shift when moving from emergency resuscitation to palliative care?

options.A: The focus shifts from invasive life-prolonging measures to symptom control and family support
options.B: The nurse stops all administration of pain medication
options.C: The nurse mandates that the patient be moved to a distant tertiary facility
options.D: The nurse stops visiting the patient entirely because no further treatment exists

explanation: End-of-life care is all about easing physical pain and wrapping the family in warm, compassionate support. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h7)

question: Who are the key local partners working alongside community nurses during an emergency?

options.A: Community health extension workers, midwives, and local transport providers
options.B: International pharmaceutical manufacturers and corporate executives
options.C: Hospital accountants and administrative billing officers

explanation: Teamwork makes the dream work! Community nurses rely closely on CHEWs, midwives, and local drivers to handle crises smoothly. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h8)

question: How does community critical care connect to wider public health goals?

options.A: By tracking disease outbreaks, educating the public, and promoting early recognition of danger signs
options.B: By replacing all national public health vaccination programs
options.C: By focusing exclusively on treating isolated patients inside locked clinic rooms
options.D: By restricting health education to urban teaching hospitals only

explanation: Community nursing goes beyond the clinic doors by keeping an eye out for outbreaks and teaching families how to spot danger early. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h8)
